utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the Registrar to call out the case number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-T Prosecutor versus Slatko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, can we have the appearances please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi, Ms. Sutherland and Mr. Vos.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, my name is Toma Fila and together with my colleagues, Petrovic and Ms. Lopicic, I will defend Zlatko Dokmanovic in these proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We can therefore start with the Prosecutor's opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a case which concerns events that started at the Vukovar hospital on 20th November 1991. It is a case about 200 Croatian and other non-Serb persons, most of them patients of that hospital who were removed from their sick beds on the morning of 20th November 1991, transported to military barracks in Vukovar and then subsequently, in the afternoon, to a collective farm, at Ovcara. It is a case where many of these patients from the hospital were severely beaten. The beatings were so severe that two of them died. It is a case where, after these horrendous beatings, and after some of them were separated out, the remainder of them were transported to a place just nearby where, in the course of the evening and night, they were summarily executed and buried in a mass grave. It is the case of Slavko Dokmanovic, the president of the municipality of Vukovar, who actively participated in the events which led to the death of these innocent victims. By virtue of his participation, Slavko Dokmanovic is charged with violations of the laws and customs of war, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, and crimes against humanity. The accused is not the only person responsible for these terrible acts. He knowingly acted in concert with others, including Mile Mrksic, Miroslav Radic, and Veselin Sljivancanin. These participants are no less culpable than the accused himself. Throughout the course of these proceedings your Honour may hear these names mentioned from time to time. The events for which the accused stands trial were part of a widespread and systematic large-scale attack against the non-Serb residents of the municipality of Vukovar. All the various stages in the chain of events which led to, and indeed ended in, the mass grave at Ovcara, form part of a well-orchestrated and continuous course of action. The acts contained in the indictment are the intentional acts, wilful acts and omissions of the accused, as the highest Serbian civilian authority in the municipality of Vukovar and his fellow commanding military and paramilitary conspirators and associates. There can be no justification for these crimes. The criminal activity that underscored these offences was on a scale that shocks the consciousness of mankind. The motivation for these murders was hatred based on prejudice and intolerance. The basis for the selection and subsequent execution of these captives was national, ethnic, religious and political. The victims were chosen by their executioners for killing because they were not the same ethnic group as the perpetrators. These innocent victims were not casualties of war, killed in the course of armed conflict, but many of them were civilians and non-combatants removed from their hospital beds and slaughtered. It is the Prosecution case that the accused is individually responsible for the crimes alleged against him in the indictment, pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Individual criminal responsibility includes committing, planning, instigating, ordering, or otherwise aiding and abetting the planning, preparation or execution of any of the crimes referred to in Articles 2-5 of the Tribunal Statute. However, the accused's criminal responsibility for the crimes committed on 20th November 1991 in and around Ovcara is not only based on his direct and active participation, but also by virtue of his position of authority, where the evidence suggests not a direct involvement, but a failure to prevent, stop, or punish such crimes. This latter responsibility, individual responsibility, for omissions -- this latter principle of individual responsibility for omissions, long recognised under international criminal law, was reaffirmed by Article 7(3) of the Statute. If I may, for a short moment, turn to the accused himself, your Honours, the accused, Slavko Dokmanovic, was born on 14th December 1949 in Trpinja in the Republic of Croatia of what then was the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. He is a graduate of the Faculty of Agriculture in Osijek which, is also in Croatia. He claims to be currently without citizenship and to have refugee status in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. He is a Serb by nationality. Before entering politics, the accused worked for almost eight years as an agricultural expert at the collective farm of Ovcara, the same place where these tragic events occurred. As such he gained an in-depth knowledge of the physical layout of Ovcara. At the occasion of the first multi-party elections in 1990, the accused Dokmanovic entered politics and was elected to the Vukovar municipal assembly as a member of the Party for Democratic Change. Subsequently, Dokmanovic was elected president of the municipal assembly. In this capacity, he carried out the executive functions of the assembly, and as such, acted as the chief executive authority in the municipality. He held this position from June 1990 until June 1991. At this time, citing fears for his safety, he refused to continue going to Vukovar, which led to the Croatian authorities to name a replacement. Even during this period when Serb forces were besieging Vukovar, the accused Dokmanovic still maintained a presence on the local political scene, and to many Serbs was considered the legitimate president of the municipal assembly. Immediately after the city of Vukovar fell to the JNA, the accused Dokmanovic resumed his role as president of the municipality for a short period, and then entered into the government of the rebel Serb autonomous region. In 1994 he resumed his position of president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar, a post he held up until April of 1996. Your Honours, the city of Vukovar is located in the Eastern Slavonian region of Croatia on the banks of the Danube River which there marks the borders between the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Croatia. The city straddles the Vuka River which flows into the Danube just north of the city centre. South-East of Vukovar the terrain consists mostly of rolling hills and bluffs along the Danube. North of Vuka, the terrain is very flat, as it is to the south and west. The area is primarily agricultural, most of the land is cultivated and there are relatively few forested areas. To assist your Honours, we have some maps prepared which we would like to take you to now, if we may, on the television screen, to indicate some of the places that we have spoken of, and with the assistance of the technician, might I ask that the first map be displayed, that being B1-1, a map of the western Vulkans area, be displayed. (Map displayed) Your Honours, this is a very large map and it is not very easy to see individual places on it, looking at it on the screen, but your Honours may be able to see that there -- the red lines mark the division between the various Republics of Yugoslavia, Bosnia, Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia, et cetera. A more precise and clear map is B1-2, and if we could have that, I think it may be easier for your Honours to see it. (Map shown) That is much clearer for your Honours. I think you can see there in the purple section towards the top the Vukovar -- is marked, and the name, "Vukovar", appears. Again, perhaps if we can now have B1-3, your Honours, this is a large map which shows the municipality of Vukovar. Your Honours well understand that there is -- the municipalities in Yugoslavia are often named after the largest towns which appear, so there is the city of Vukovar and the municipality of Vukovar. That is a consistent pattern that runs across the whole of Yugoslavia. Finally, if we could have B1-4 on the screen. (Map shown). This, your Honour, is a more expanded version of the map that we have just had. Your Honours can see clearly there the city of Vukovar, and if I ask the technician, he might kindly mark that for us, and because these events are so concerned with the collective farm at Ovcara, I would ask the technician if he would be so kind to put a marking there. You can see the pin mark now appearing. That gives you the relative distance of Vukovar to Ovcara. Thank you very much. In the 1991 census, the population of the Vukovar municipality was 84,189 persons, of which 36,910 were Croats (43.8 per cent), 31,445 were Serb (37.4 per cent), 1,375 were Hungarian (1.6 per cent), 6,124 were Yugoslavian (7.3 per cent), and 8,335, being "others", were 9.9 per cent. During World War II the region around Vukovar was relatively peaceful and it seems to have escaped much of the ethnic fighting which occurred in other areas of Yugoslavia. After the war, however, the significant ethnic German population were forced from the region by the Tito government, leading to an influx of settlers from other parts of Yugoslavia. Some of the newcomers were forcibly sent to Eastern Slavonia but most, apparently, came on their own, from the poorer areas of Krajina, these were primarily Serb people, and from Herzegovina, and these were primarily Croats. They were seeking the rich farmland for which the area was known. In 1991, the year that the charged events took place, Vukovar was a prosperous town in Croatia, due primarily to its location as a service centre for the surrounding areas, and it was reputed to be the richest farmland in all of the former Yugoslavia. The regional economy was also supplemented by nearby oil and natural gas deposits, as well as by the large Borovo factory which employed thousands of persons and manufactured shoes, leather and rubber goods. Your Honours, we have a short video which video the Defence have. We have taken very short excerpts of it to show the city of Vukovar as it was before the siege, and if I could ask the technicians in the booth to kindly play that video, in segments 1, 2 and 3. (Video played). "Scenes of Vukovar prior to the battle". Understand, your Honours, that most of these scenes were shot in the early part of 1991. Perhaps if the technicians could fast forward now slightly onto the final segment, it is segment 3. If that can be done very quickly, otherwise we will move on. (Video played). This, your Honours, as I understand, is a shot of the agricultural lands surrounding Vukovar. Thank you. I think that is enough. Your Honours, the ethnic tension first manifested itself in the Vukovar region in early 1991. The atmosphere of tension was exacerbated by Serbian and Croatian radicals, who visited the area calling for violent responses to the other side's "provocations". On both sides the introduction of more and more well-armed ultra-nationalists caused the situation to deteriorate. An incident on 2nd May 1991 when 12 Croatian policemen were shot in the neighbouring village of Borovo Selo marked the beginning of the slide into armed conflict in the region and from the time of that incident on, there were gun battles occurring between the Serbs and the Croats on an increasingly regular basis. After the referendum of 17th May 1991, the Republic of Croatia decided to no longer remain in the Socialist Federation of Yugoslavia, so it declared its independence on 25th June 1991, but at the urging of the European Community the effective date of independence was postponed for three months until 8th October 1991. Croatia's transition from a Federal Republic to that of an independent state in its own right was not smooth or free of conflict. In August of 1991, after attacking some of the surrounding villages, the JNA, the Yugoslavia People's Army, laid siege to the city of Vukovar. On 25th August 1991, the JNA launched a full-scale assault on Vukovar, including land, air and naval forces, which were all utilised in a co-ordinated attack. The battle of Vukovar lasted just short of three months and resulted in great damage to the city, and to the death of many hundreds of persons. Ultimately Vukovar fell on 18th November 1991. The JNA and the Serb paramilitary forces occupied what remained of the city. The remaining Croatian defenders surrendered, although significant numbers of them were killed on the spot, or were executed shortly thereafter. We have now some scenes on the video relating to that battle and to the city and aftermath of the battle, and if segments 4 and 5 could now be shown on the screen, these segments, if your Honours please, relate to the siege of Vukovar and its aftermath. (Video played). "Scenes of Vukovar during and in the aftermath of the battle". Thank you. Your Honours, by the time the city fell, the JNA had amassed in excess of 30,000 troops in the Vukovar area. These JNA forces were joined by significant numbers of Serb regular troops, coming from Territorial Defence units, as well as volunteers in paramilitary units who had flocked to the area from Serbia, Montenegro and the Serbian regions of Croatia. The Serbian units with primary responsibility for the attack and subsequent occupation of Vukovar was the Belgrade-based Guards Brigade, commanded by Colonel Mile Mrksic. Subordinate to Colonel Mrksic was Major Veselin Sljivancanin, who had direct operational command of JNA forces in the immediate area of the city. Major Sljivancanin was the commanding officer for the Belgrade Guards, and he also commanded a military police battalion which was part of the brigade. Another part of the brigade that took an active role in the siege and occupation of the city was the special infantry unit commanded by Captain Miroslav Radic, a close associate of Major Sljivancanin. Your Honours, the Vukovar hospital is located in the centre of the city. The hospital was well signposted, on its roof was painted a large red cross, and a big linen Red Cross sign was displayed in the courtyard of the hospital, but instead of being saved from bombardment, including aerial bombardment, the hospital was constantly attacked. Notwithstanding the constant shelling throughout the course of the siege, the Vukovar hospital kept functioning. Chief physician and director of the hospital, Dr. Bosanac, who will give evidence in these proceedings, maintained contact with the outside world and international organisations. Dr. Bosanac was instrumental in planning for the sick and wounded of the hospital to be evacuated under the supervision of the European Community Monitoring Mission and the International Committee of the Red Cross. There are some short video segments of this process of evacuation that was arranged and organised by Dr. Bosanac, and if we could see briefly those segments now, 6, 7 and 8. (Video played). The first part shows the hospital and then the second part goes on to the evacuation itself. By the time the city surrendered, many of the Croatian/Serbian people who had been trapped in Vukovar by the JNA siege had assembled in the Vukovar hospital, where several hundred people gathered in the belief that it would be evacuated in the presence of neutral, international observers. In addition to the sick and wounded, civilian families and families of hospital staff, and soldiers who had been defending the city, some posing as patients or hospital staff, gathered in the hospital and on the hospital grounds. I think we now have that on the screen, your Honours, so perhaps if that could be played. (Video played). On 18th November 1991 representatives of the Republic of Croatia, the JNA, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and other international humanitarian bodies reached an agreement regarding a convoy to evacuate the wounded and sick from the Vukovar hospital, which contained a guarantee of a cease-fire during the period of the evacuation, an agreement to provide suitable vehicles, recognition of the neutrality of the Vukovar hospital during the evacuation period, and the placing of the hospital staff under the protection of the International Committee of the Red Cross. The agreement was followed by more detailed memorandum of understanding in which the signatories agreed that all wounded and sick combatants would be treated in accordance with Geneva Conventions I and II, and that all captured combatants would be treated in accordance with Geneva Convention III, and that all civilians would be treated in accordance with Articles 70 to 149 of Geneva Convention IV, including the grave breach provisions of Article 147. On the afternoon of 19th of November 1991, Major Veselin Sljivancanin entered the hospital with the JNA units and assumed control. Early in the morning of 20th November 1991, Major Sljivancanin ordered the nurses and doctors of the hospital to assemble for a meeting in the basement of the hospital. Meanwhile, on the orders of Major Sljivancanin, a list of all those present at the hospital had been prepared. During the meeting of the medical staff, the JNA and Serb paramilitary soldiers separated the men from the women. By the time the medical staff meeting with Major Sljivancanin had concluded, the soldiers had removed almost all the men who were at the hospital using the list that had been prepared previously. Among those removed in this way were wounded patients, hospital staff, soldiers who had been defending the city, Croatian political activists and other civilians. No regard was had to the fact that the majority of the men patients were sick or wounded. Many of them bore wound drains, plaster casts and medical paraphernalia. The soldiers loaded about 300 of these men onto five or six civilian buses and held them on the buses under guard. Later that morning, the buses left the hospital compound and proceeded through the centre of Vukovar to the JNA barracks on the south side of the city. The men were kept inside the buses at the barracks for about two hours. During that time, at least fifteen of the men were removed from the buses, apparently because these men were part of the hospital staff or who were related to staff members. Those who had to remain on the buses were then verbally abused and threatened. Survivors of this bus journey will testify before this Chamber. Around noon or shortly thereafter, the remainder of the men were then driven to a building at the Ovcara farm about four kilometres south-east of Vukovar. Your Honours, for your assistance we have had prepared, and this has been disclosed to the Defence as well, a very short video segment showing the route that was taken from the hospital compound to the JNA barracks, and then subsequently from the JNA barracks to the Ovcara hangar. These are video segments 9 and 10, and if they could be played, please. (Video played). That is the hospital, your Honours. That spot marks the JNA barracks, your Honours. From that spot, your Honours, they then go from the JNA barracks out to the collective farm at Ovcara where the buses halt at a hangar. Your Honours, the JNA and Serb paramilitary soldiers took -- we are now being shown the short distance from the hangar to the grave, your Honours. The JNA and Serb paramilitary soldiers took the men from the buses and forced them to run between two lines of soldiers to the entrance of the hangar. As they passed, the men were severely beaten. Once inside the hangar, the men were ordered to stand and face the wall, or sit down on the ground. The evidence will show that what had happened, thus far, was only a prelude to scenes of unimaginable cruelty and brutality. The men were beaten for several hours. This was done in a systematic way. JNA and paramilitary soldiers would come into the hangar from outside and start to beat and kick the people inside severely. As they got tired, the beaters were replaced by others who had fresh energy to continue the beatings. The evidence will show that at least two of the men in the hangar did not survive. The accused was present at these beatings for an extended period of time. The evidence will demonstrate that he paced up and down the hangar and acted in a position of authority. The accused also singled out certain individuals who were subsequently beaten even more severely. About seven of the men were released. Seven of the victims were released after Serbs intervened on their behalf. These men were removed from the hangar in which the beatings took place, and assembled outside. Later on, they were driven back to Vukovar. The Prosecution will call evidence from one of these survivors who will testify that the soldiers who intervened on his behalf knew that those who remained at the farm were to be killed. The accused, Dokmanovic, was present when these men were saved. The accused was also present as final preparation were being made for the execution, acts which signalled clearly what the fate of the captives would be. He was present as preparation were being made in all openness for ensuring mass execution. To this end, the Prosecution will adduce evidence in relation to the steps taken to prepare the mass grave. Thereafter, identifying information about each man was listed, and then the men were divided into groups of 10-20. Each group was loaded in turn onto a truck, which left the farm building with that group, and then returned empty a short while later. Clearly, these events, in their entirety, demonstrate that those at the Ovcara hangar, including the accused, were well aware of the up-coming execution, and by his actions and presence, the accused was an integral part of the preparation thereto. The truck that transported the captives to their death travelled south from the Ovcara building on the road leading to Grabovo. Approximately one and one-tenth kilometres south-west of the building, the vehicle turned left and then travelled north-east on a dirt field road which ran between a cultivated field on the left, and a wooded ravine on the right. The sole survivor of this fateful journey, and whose testimony we will hear in the course of these proceedings; one man managed to leap undetected from one of the truck. He is the last survivor on what was the road to a summary cruel and certain death. At the end of the ravine, approximately 900 metres from the Ovcara/Grabovo road, the soldiers removed the men from the truck. At this spot, JNA and Serb paramilitary troops were assembled on the north side of the site where a mass grave site had been prepared. During the evening hours of 20th November 1991, these soldiers, firing in a southerly direction, shot and killed, or otherwise killed, at least 198 men and two women. The remains of these men have since been exhumed from the place where the executions took place. The Prosecution will produce numerous exhibits which provide painstaking documentation and a poignant and grisly testimonial of the crimes that were there committed. The Prosecution will show that the accused's participation in the beatings, and his presence and his actions with respect to the planning and implementation of the mass execution, are criminal offences under Article 7(1) of the Statute, and that his failure to prevent the violations as a superior results in criminal liability under Article 7(3) of the Statute. Your Honours, the final demonstration that I wish to show you is a map, B1-6, and on that map I wish to show you some of the towns that may be referred to during the course of the evidence. It is an expanded map of the Vukovar municipality and contains some of the well-known places, and with the assistance of the technicians, could that be displayed now, please? (Map shown). It appears on the computer monitor. Your Honours, I would ask the technician to mark these towns quickly for me, if he would; Vukovar, Vinkovci -- you cannot see all of Vinkovci, your Honours, but it is where it is being marked now. Ovcara, Borovo, and Trpinja. And last but not at least, Ilok. If your Honours please: Now turning to the indictment itself, the accused in this case, Slavko Dokmanovic is charged with some six counts in the indictment. The charges are grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, violations to the laws and customs of war, and crimes against humanity. Counts 1, 2 and 3 are concerned primarily with the beatings that took place in the farm building at Ovcara, and counts 4, 5 and 6 are primarily concerned with murder, or are concerned with the murders that took place at the grave site. None of the counts are in the alternative, the counts are cumulative. Turning now to grave breaches. The accused is charged with grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions under Article 2 of our Statute. The common element of grave breaches is that the victims are persons protected by one of the Geneva Conventions, that the actions or omissions occurred during an armed conflict or partial or total occupation, in which the laws for international armed conflict applies. The jurisdictional prerequisite then, with respect to Article 2, is that the conflict must be shown to have been international in character, and that the victims were persons protected by the Geneva Conventions. These elements are derived from the 1949 Conventions. The Appeals Chamber held that Article 2 of the Statute is based on the Geneva Conventions of 1949, and more specifically, the provisions of those Conventions relating to grave breaches of the Conventions. As previously stated, it is the Prosecution position that at all relevant times a state of international armed conflict existed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. At all relevant times all victims were protected by the Geneva Conventions of 1949, and, at all relevant times, the accused was required to abide by the laws and customs governing the conduct of war, including the Geneva Conventions of 1949. With respect to the question of internationality, in order for the Geneva Conventions to be operative, the internationality requirement must be fulfilled. Croatia had declared its independence in June 1991, and although this was initially suspended at the request of the international community, it did become effective from 8th October 1991 and well before the events in this case. This was a war waged by the government of Yugoslavia in Belgrade against an independent Croatia, thus a war between two sovereign states; or an international conflict for the purposes of the Convention. It is therefore the Prosecution's position that, at all relevant times, the armed conflict in Vukovar was one between two separate states which were unambiguously international in character. At all relevant times, the JNA were the military force representing the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and were under the command and direction of Yugoslavia authorities in Belgrade. This military entity was supported by other Serbian forces and paramilitaries. The antagonists were the forces of the Republic of Croatia. They constitute approximately 1800 men who had been loosely formed into a volunteer Defence force for the city. At first, this force was poorly organised and contained few professional soldiers. However, it organised itself in time into a more effective unit within the structure of an infantry brigade with a clear chain of command and with designated areas of responsibility. The Croatian forces also included policemen from the Croatian Ministry of the Interior, and, as tensions rose in the area, the Croatian authorities also despatched significant numbers of the Croatian National Guard. The two sides were clearly drawn. Each side with a military presence under the directives of a distinct state. As such, the conflict meets the requirements of internationality, and in accordance with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions, the laws governing international armed conflict continue to apply until conclusion of peace is reached. Touching briefly, if I may, on armed conflict itself, in order to invoke the operation of the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions, a conflict must not only be international but it must be "armed". These provisions apply to protected persons only to the extent that they are the subject of an armed conflict. There is no doubt that at all relevant times in Vukovar there existed a conflict of sufficient intensity and organisation to amount to an armed conflict. From late August 1991, the city of Vukovar was subjected to a massive land, naval, and air offensive by forces of the JNA, assisted by various Serbian paramilitary groups. Despite the organisation of armed resistance, the city of Vukovar was captured around the 18th November 1991, after intense shelling and a siege of almost three months. Clearly, the events arising out of the indictment against the accused occurred during the course of an international armed conflict. The second requirement, then, in order to invoke the grave breaches provisions, is the requirement that the victims of the offences committed be "protected persons". According to the Appeals Chamber, it is the status of the victim as a "protected person" that makes the grave breach provisions operative. It was decided in the Tadic decision on jurisdiction that: "Offences under Article 2 can only be prosecuted when perpetrated against persons or property regarded as 'protected' by the Geneva Conventions under the strict conditions set out by the Conventions themselves." The Prosecution's evidence will demonstrate that the victims in the present case are protected persons under Geneva Conventions I, III, or IV. Under these Conventions, three categories of protected persons are established, specifically civilians, prisoners of war, and wounded combatants and medical staff. The requirement specified for each category will now be considered. Turning firstly to "civilian", Article 4 of the Geneva Convention IV, defines those civilians who fall under the protection of that Convention, "protected persons", are those who: "... at a given moment and in any manner whatsoever, find themselves, in the case of a conflict or occupation, in the hands of a party to the conflict or occupying power of which they are not nationals." In general terms, the categories of persons intended to be covered as civilians are "enemy nationals" in an international armed conflict, or alternatively, "the whole population of occupied territories, excluding nationals of the occupying power". In the Opinion and Judgement rendered in the Tadic case on 7th May 1997, Trial Chamber II found implicit in the definition a requirement that the victims were "in the hands of" a "party to the conflict or occupying power", and that the civilian victims were not nationals of the party or occupying power. This raises the issue of nationality of the victims, vis-à-vis the perpetrator, and implicitly, the proviso that persons are protected by this provision only to the extent that they are caught up in an international conflict. In the opinion of the International Committee of the Red Cross "commentary on Geneva Conventions IV", cited with approval by the Trial Chamber in the Tadic case, says that: "The expression, 'in the hands of', is used in an extremely general sense... the expression... need not necessarily be understood in the physical sense; it seems that the person in the territory under the control of the power in question." As such, persons removed from the Vukovar hospital and subjected to these acts specified in the indictment were undoubtedly "in the hands of" the occupying power. They were under the control of an enemy power which was comprised almost exclusively of Serb soldiers of the JNA in concert with paramilitary forces originating in the Republic of Serbia and augmented by local Serbs. These captured persons, none of whom were Serbian nationals, included wounded patients, hospital staff and other civilians, who had sought refuge in the hospital. As civilians captured after the JNA siege on Vukovar, they were clearly "protected persons" under the Fourth Geneva Convention. Turning now to "prisoners of war", Article 4 of the Geneva Convention III defines prisoners of war who are to be protected. Among the list of categories of persons included are members of armed forces, militia groups and volunteer corps. Accordingly, the Prosecution will call evidence to show that some of the victims of the Ovcara massacre were Croatian or non-Serb soldiers who had been defending the city and who had taken refuge at the hospital and who came into enemy hands when Vukovar fell to the JNA forces. The next category, "wounded and sick combatants or medical personnel". The status of wounded and sick combatants as protected persons is covered by Article 13 of Geneva Convention I, which sets out those categories of persons to be protected in times of war. Here again the categories of persons included are members of the armed forces, militia groups and volunteer corps. However, those medical persons are assigned the status of "protected person" under two separate Articles of the convention. Clearly, then, all persons removed from the Vukovar hospital that served an armed force or militia group, or voluntary corps, or who were hospital staff engaged in either the care of civilians or wounded combatants, enjoyed the status of protected persons. Accepting that there existed at the relevant time an international armed conflict, and that the persons taken from Vukovar hospital were protected for the purposes of the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions, I now turn to the charges themselves. The accused has been charged with aiding and abetting or otherwise participating in both wilfully causing great suffering to and wilfully killing persons removed from the Vukovar hospital. The relevant provisions are as follows; wilful killing is dealt with by Article 2(A), and the elements of these offences are: that the victim is dead; that the death resulted from an unlawful act or omission in which the accused -- act or omission of the accused; and at the time of the acts or omissions, the accused (or a subordinate), had the intent to kill or inflict grievous bodily harm on the victim. Where an accused acts with the intent to commit grievous bodily harm, the accused possesses the requisite mens rea for a wilful killing if death in fact results. One who intends to inflict serious bodily injury necessarily acts in reckless disregard of the possibility that death might result. However, the offence of wilful killing is not limited to the commission of positive acts, as the term "wilful" encompasses the element of recklessness. A wilful omission intended to cause death qualifies as a wilful killing. For example, allowing protected persons in detention to starve to death or letting wounded persons die for want of crucial medical care could both be considered as wilful killings. Now, wilfully causing great suffering, Article 2(C) in the Statute, prohibits wilfully causing great suffering and the elements are: that the accused (or a subordinate) committed a specified act or omission upon the victim; that the accused (or a subordinate) committed the act or omission with the intention of unlawfully inflicting great suffering; and finally, that suffering was thereby inflicted. In the context of the events at Ovcara and the criminal offences that give rise to this indictment, there is ample evidence to support each of these elements. In addition, it seems that the "great suffering" inflicted is of both a physical and a mental nature. Clearly the facts disclose evidence of both physical torment and mental anguish. This is not precluded by the wording of the Statute, as the Conventions do not limit the term, "great suffering" to physical suffering. In fact, the International Committee of the Red Cross commentary on the Geneva Convention IV states that: "Since the Conventions do not specify that only physical suffering is meant, it can quite legitimately be held to cover mental sufferings also." Accordingly, the scope of "great suffering" includes acts or omissions intended to cause mental suffering as well as physical evidence of abuse. This has a particular relevance to the facts in issue here, for effectively the suffering borne by the victims at Ovcara began at the Vukovar hospital and continued until their untimely death at the Ovcara grave site. In effect, the verbal taunting and threats of death led the victims to be in constant fear for their lives, a fear that was ultimately realised. The physical suffering sustained by protracted beatings is of course the more obvious basis for the charge of great suffering. These beatings, the witnesses will tell, lasted for hours. The solders took rotations on the prompting of a whistle. There can be no doubt that the brutal battering and unrestrained violence that took place in the Ovcara farm hangar, and that resulted in the death of at least two of the victims, constitutes "suffering" on a great scale. Turning now to the violations of the laws and customs of war, in relation to the violations of the laws or customs of war, counts 2 and 5, Article 3 of the Statute provides that the Tribunal shall have the power to prosecute persons violating the laws or customs of war, and specifically states that the enumerated offences in paragraphs (a)-(e) are not exhaustive. In addition to other codifications of the laws and customs of war, common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, and the 1977 Additional Protocols I and II are included within the parameters of the Statute. Further, there are recognised minimum rules applicable to all armed conflicts, regardless of their classification, which the enumerated offences in common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions apply. As the Appeal Chamber in the Tadic case noted, Article 3 confers on the International Tribunal, jurisdiction over serious offences against international humanitarian law, not covered by Articles 2, 4, or 5. The Appeals Chamber then specified the jurisdictional prerequisites which must be met for offences to be subject to prosecution under Article 3 of the Statute. In the present case, the accused is charged under Article 3 with murder and cruel treatment. These come within the purview of Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute on the basis of common Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions. The Appeals Chamber has recognised that under international customary law the rules set forth in common Article 3 reflect "elementary considerations of humanity", applicable to all armed conflicts whether internal or international. The provisions of common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions prohibit particular acts, including, "violence to life and persons, in particular murder of all kinds [and] cruel treatment", when committed "at any time and in any place whatsoever", against: "Persons taking no active part in hostilities, including members of the armed forces who have laid down their arms and those placed hors de combat by sickness, wounds, detention, or any other cause [who] shall in all circumstances by treated humanely, without any adverse distinction founded on race, colour, religion or faith, sex, birth or wealth, or any other similar criteria." Accordingly, taking into account the rules of international customary law, and the provisions of common Article 3, in order to prove a violation of common Article 3, the Prosecutor must and will show beyond a reasonable doubt that: (i) the unlawful acts were committed in the context of an armed conflict; (ii) the accused was connected to one side involved in the armed conflict; (iii) the victims were persons taking no active part (or no longer taking part) in hostilities, which includes civilians, members of the armed forces who have laid down their arms, and those placed hors de combat by sickness, wounds, detention, or any other cause; (iv) the accused committed one of the enumerated acts listed in common Article 3 of the Geneva Convention. Turning, then, to cruel treatment, common Article 3 deals with cruel treatment and the elements of that offence are: that the accused (or a subordinate) committed a specified act or omission against the victim; the victim was a non-combatant or hors de combat; and that the accused (or subordinate) thereby intended to subject the victim to cruel treatment. Put simply, an act or omission is cruel if the accused was indifferent to or gratified by the victim's suffering. Common Article 3(1) stipulates that all persons taking no active part in hostilities shall be treated humanely. To this end, common Article 3(1)(a) prohibits, "violence to life and person, in particular murder of all kinds, mutilation, cruel treatment and torture". It is submitted by the Prosecution that "cruel treatment" encompasses situations where the accused intentionally and severely mistreats another person, as in this case, the beating at the Ovcara farm. Under this charge it is sufficient that the accused intentionally subjects the captives to cruelty. He need not have been -- he need not have had the underlying purpose of torture or the intent to cause great suffering or serious injury to body or health. As such, the alleged acts contained in this indictment have little difficulty in meeting the required elements of this charge. Murder, under common Article 3. The elements are: that the victim is dead; the victim was a non-combatant or hors de combat; that the death resulted from an unlawful act or omission in which the accused (or a subordinate) participated; and at the time of the killing the accused (or a subordinate) had the intent to kill or inflict grievous bodily harm. Common Article 3(1)(a) prohibits "murder of all kinds" committed against persons taking no active part in hostilities. While some national systems distinguish between murder and other forms of wilful killing, no such distinction is appropriate in the context of the Geneva Conventions. Finally, the crimes against humanity. Under Article 5, the Statute confers jurisdiction in relation to crimes against humanity. The Article lists the enumerated offences. The statement of the offences establishes the basic elements of crimes against humanity as serious inhumane acts directed against any civilian population when committed in armed conflict, whether international or internal in character. In the case at hand the accused is charged with crimes against humanity, counts 3 and 6. These are serious offences directed against person as part of a widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population. The victims of crimes against humanity constitute a wider class than those who are covered by Articles 2 and 3 in the Statute of the Tribunal, and may include fellow citizens of the person committing offences as well as stateless persons. Crimes against humanity can be distinguished from genocide in that they do not require an intent to destroy the group, only proof that the act was part of a widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population. The common element is that the act or omission was part of a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population. This will be established by the Prosecution in several ways. First, by expert testimony which will provide the court with a perspective of the wide-ranging attack by the JNA on several fronts in Croatia. Secondly, you will hear the testimony of several persons who will describe the siege against the city of Vukovar and the manner in which the Serb forces utilised artillery to destroy the city. Finally, you will hear testimony related to the Vukovar hospital incident alone which will show that 200 persons were murdered, some of them young boys, some of them elderly and incapacitated, and some women. The following elements are the common elements for violations of Article 5: (i) that the act or omission in question must be committed in the context of an armed conflict, which can be internal or international in character; (ii) that there must be a sufficient nexus between those acts or omissions and the armed conflict; (iii) that the acts or omissions must be part of an ongoing widespread or systematic occurrence of crimes directed against civilian population; and, (iv) that the accused committed one of the acts enumerated in Article 5. In relation to the requirement that the acts or omissions be committed in the context of an armed conflict, the test to be applied is that stated by the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic decision on jurisdiction, when it held that: "An armed conflict exists whenever there is resort to armed force between States or protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups, or between groups within a State." Thus, Article 5 may be invoked as a basis of jurisdiction over crimes committed in either international or internal armed conflicts. With respect to the scope of the nexus between the armed conflict and the act or omission requirement, it is sufficient for a violation of Article 5 to demonstrate that the crimes were committed at some point in the course or duration of an armed conflict, even if such crimes were not committed in direct relation to or as part of the conduct of hostilities, occupation, or other integral aspects of the armed conflict. The term, "population", in Article 5 contemplates that by his actions the accused participated in a widespread or systematic attack against a relatively large victim group as distinct from isolated or random acts against individuals. This is certainly the situation in this case. The elements of murder under Article 5 are again: that the victim is dead; the death resulted from an unlawful act or omission of the accused (or a subordinate); and that at the time of the killing the accused (or a subordinate) had the intent to kill or inflict grievous bodily harm on the victim. Inhumane acts under Article 5(1), the elements of that offence are: that the accused (or a subordinate) committed a specific act or omission against the victim; that the act or omission of the accused (or a subordinate) was unlawful. The Report of the Secretary-General on the Statute of the Tribunal indicates that Article 5 contemplates, "inhumane acts of a very serious nature", and comments, by way of example, that in the former Yugoslavia, "such inhumane acts have taken the form of so-called 'ethnic cleansing', and widespread and systematic rape and other forms of sexual assault, including enforce prostitution." Turning now, your Honours, briefly, to individual responsibility, under Article 7(1) this Statute, the accused is individually responsible for the crimes alleged against him pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute. Individual criminal responsibility includes committing, planning, instigating, ordering, or otherwise aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation, or execution of any crimes referred to in Articles 2-5 of the Statute. In support of the Prosecution's case, several identification witnesses will be presented, who will place the accused Dokmanovic at key positions and will identify him with key roles in the beatings at Ovcara and in the events leading up to the mass killing at Ovcara, demonstrating his participation in these crimes, both direct and indirect. Dealing now with the question of intent and direct contribution, in the Tadic decision of 7th May 1997, the Trial Chamber found that various patterns emerged from a reading of the World War II cases which established that for a finding of criminal responsibility as an accessory, there must be intent on the part of the accused, and a direct contribution to the commission of the offence. More often than not in the relevant case law, the intent was established through a showing of knowledge of the criminal nature of the act on the part of the accused. But knowing that a certain course of action was criminal and by then wilfully associating oneself with the acts or its consequences, the accused indicated his intent and his, "conscious decision to participate by planning, instigating, ordering, committing, or otherwise aiding and abetting in the commission of a crime". Superior responsibility under Article 7(3) is also charged in the indictment. The Prosecution will show that the accused has is also criminally liable for not preventing or stopping the beatings and killings at Ovcara while he was in a position to do so, because he was able to exercise control over the people who participated in committing those beatings and killings. Accordingly, the Prosecution also contends that the accused is criminally liable under Article 7(3) of the Statute. It is the Prosecution's position that a "superior" within the meaning of this provision includes civilian superior. What is essential is that someone who holds authority over others who are about to commit acts described in Articles 2-5 of the Statute, prevents them from doing so or punishes them if the acts have already been committed. The Prosecution will show that the accused failed in this obligation. In order to establish criminal liability under Article 7(3) of the Statute, the Prosecution must show three requirements: first it must show that the accused held a position which was superior; secondly, the Prosecution must show that the accused had actual knowledge of the crimes that were to take place or had taken place, or that he should have been aware of the crimes, and third and last, that the Prosecution must show that the accused did not take the necessary measures to prevent the crimes, or punish the perpetrators thereof. The Prosecution will show that all of these requirements have been satisfied. Until July 1991, the accused was the president of the Vukovar municipal assembly and as such the highest civilian authority in the municipality. Upon his arrival in Vukovar after the fighting ended on 19th November 1991, when the city was in the control of the Serbs, he assumed his former position as if nothing had changed. It should be noted that even in the period leading up to and during the siege of the city, between June and November 1991, the accused Dokmanovic continued to act as the president of Serb Vukovar. In relation to an operation on the scale of the execution of 200-odd people, it is obvious that a vast amount of preparation and planning was necessary. Various stages have to be included in the planning, and the logistical support necessary for the operation which had -- and resources had to be marshalled. The meeting called by Major Sljivancanin at the hospital which ensured that the hospital staff could not obstruct the removal of the detainees; the brief detention at the JNA barracks; the more extended detention at the Ovcara farm; the selection and preparation of the execution site; the transfer of the detainees to the site in manageable groups; the selection of the soldiers who were to carry out the executions; the excavation of a mass grave; the executions themselves, and the burial; the transport between each of these points also had to be arranged in advance. Finally, all these steps had to be carried out in utmost secrecy so that no interruptions or resistance would be encountered. The accused was present at Ovcara farm at the time of the beatings which took place over a period of several hours. Furthermore, he actively participated in these beatings. This direct participation in these acts by the accused is, in the Prosecution's submission, sufficient to convict him on counts, 1, 2 and 3 on the indictment. In relation to the killings caused by the beatings at the farm, it is also clear from the World War II cases and from the decision in Tadic that the accused's actions were sufficient to ensure conviction on counts 4, 5 and 6. In the trial of Franz Schonfeld and Nine Others, the Judge Advocate, in setting out the law applicable to accessories, states at one point: "The accessory is, however, liable, for all that ensues upon the execution of an unlawful act commanded; that is to say, if A commands B to beat C, and B beats C so that he dies, A is an accessory to the murder of C. There must be some active proceeding on the part of the accessory, that is, he must procure, incite or in some other way encourage the act done by the principal." The accused Dokmanovic's active participation in the beating of detainees, even if they were not the ones to be killed by the beatings, themselves constitute encouragement of the unlawful actions of the principals to the murder of the two detainees. His mere presence in relation to the beatings of the two detainees who were thus killed could be construed as encouragement. In terms of the execution itself, the role of the accused in the preparation of the killings has been set out above. Because of his connection to the crime through a variety of means, his presence at the execution site at the time of the executions is not necessary for convictions for the killings that took place there. It is important to emphasise that the events described above and the separation of the detainees from the hospital staff to the burial of the victims all took place on one day; 20th November 1991. The distance from the hospital to the execution site was no more than five or six kilometres. These events were neither telescoped out in time nor in space, and cannot and should not be seen as discrete and disconnected, but rather as one continuous transaction, the culmination of which was the wooded ravine and the mass grave. It is inconceivable that someone in the position of the accused could not have fully grasped the import of what was happening that day, with the frenzy of activity that had to have been taking place. His direct participation in the beating of the prisoners alone, no more than one or two hours from their terrible deaths, inextricably connects him with a criminal enterprise, the purpose of which was known to him and agreed to by him. That the purpose of the enterprise was known to all of those present at the farm is clear from the fact that a group of seven prisoners was removed from the rest of the group and they were told that they were to be saved. The evidence was thus established that the impending execution of the detainees was common knowledge. The evidence will also show that the accused conducted himself in the hangar at Ovcara in such a way as to convey the impression that he was a person in authority. According to the requirements just enumerated, it must have first of all be established that the accused was in the position of a civilian superior in respect of those who carried out the beatings and killings at Ovcara. In this respect, it is decisive whether the superior had control over those who committed the crimes. This control may be direct or indirect de facto or de jure. The Prosecution will show that the accused was indeed in the position of a civilian superior. First of all, the accused was president of the assembly, prior to the start of the hostilities. The authority of the municipal assembly of Vukovar was not limited to Vukovar itself, but comprised considerable surrounding area of some 600-odd square kilometres. This included a number of towns and villages, such as Ilok, Trpinja -- where the accused lived, Negoslavci -- where the JNA had its headquarters, and Ovcara itself. All events alleged in the indictment took place within this area. As president of the municipal assembly, the accused wielded considerable authority, also over the executive council of the municipal assembly, which body was charged with implementing the decisions of the municipal assembly. Throughout the siege of Vukovar, which began in August 1991, the accused continued to act as mayor remember of Serb Vukovar. He also, by his own account, took a position as Minister of Agriculture in the "Government of the Serb Autonomous Region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Sirmium", an office which would have given him purview over the Ovcara farm facilities where these crimes were committed. From his office in Erdut, north of Vukovar, he would have wielded considerable influence as a central figure in regional government. In the period leading up to and in the immediate aftermath of the fall of Vukovar, the accused's leadership role became clearly apparent. He participated in a number of high-level meetings with other officials in Erdut on 19th November and in the Backa Palanka on 20th. Also on 20th November, the accused by his own account, travelled to Vukovar in an official delegation which had no problem entering the area which the JNA still described as a war zone. In the following days, the accused gave television interviews in which he was referred to as, the president of the municipality. Significantly, one of these interviews was conducted by a reporter from Serbian television who addressed the accused Dokmanovic as, "the president of the assembly".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mayor, sorry. A title which is not protested or corrected by the accused. It is clear from all of this that the accused, despite any concurrent roles that he might have had in the regional government, still was viewed by others as president [sic] of Vukovar assembly, an idea which he made no attempt to dispel. Additionally the evidence will show that while present at Ovcara, Dokmanovic's authority was even more enhanced. Several witnesses have noted that the accused wore a in military uniform. According to many of the witnesses, there were both JNA and paramilitary soldiers present at Ovcara. In order to establish liability under paragraph 3 of Article 7, it is also necessary to show that the accused knew or had reason to know that the acts took place at Ovcara were being committed, were about to be committed, or had been committed. Witnesses for the Prosecution saw the accused at Ovcara farm, standing at the entrance of the hangar, pacing up and down inside the hangar, and participating in the beatings. Accordingly, it must be said that during the beatings at Ovcara, the accused was aware that they took place. He was not only participating in the crimes himself, but also, being someone holding considerable authority, giving an example for the others to follow. At that point he was fully aware of the massive scale of the beatings and of the number of people who were participating in them. Turning now to the duty to prevent or stop the crimes, as provided for under Article 7(3) it is necessary to show that the accused did not prevent the crimes from happening, while he was aware that they would take place, or that he did not punish the perpetrators after the acts had been committed. The evidence will show that the accused did nothing to prevent the beatings from continuing when he was at Ovcara. Quite the contrary. While wielding authority, as he did, he was actively participating in these events. As a high civilian official it would certainly have been possible for him to mitigate the violence that was taking place, or to spare at least some of the victims from their fate. His presence there, his leadership appearance, his singling-out of certain victims, clearly demonstrates that he did not have the least intention to prevent the crimes from being committed and going on. Also, while fully aware that the victims would be killed afterwards, the accused did nothing to alter the course of things that were to happen. In the course of the Prosecution's case, the Prosecution will call witnesses who will establish the accused's role as a civilian official, a number of witnesses who will relate to the court the events of the 20th November 1991 at the hospital, at the JNA barracks, and then the very few men lucky enough to escape and survive the hangar at Ovcara. Additional witnesses will detail the investigation into these events, the discovery of the mass grave which the Serb authorities tried so hard to conceal, and finally the exhumation of the grave itself -- an exhumation which laid bare the enormity of this crime in which at least 200 unarmed persons, many of them wounded, were brutally beaten and killed in cold blood. Numerous photographs, videotapes, slides, and ballistic evidence will also be adduced, all of which will carefully sketch the events which occurred at Ovcara; events which, owing to their very nature, left us very few survivors able to give direct eyewitness accounts. Instead, you must permit these victims to speak posthumously; and for the truth to emerge through the work of our forensic experts and through the testimonies of those left behind. The counts on the indictment that are cumulative, are cumulative and not in the alternative. The notion of cumulative charging is especially relevant in this jurisdiction, having regard to the classification of the various offences. The cumulative counts on the indictment are not duplicitous, provided they are charged on separate counts on the indictment. It may be that the facts of a particular case arising out of a single incident, could give rise to a prosecution for a number of events which may even be contained in the same provision, but providing the offences are not charged in the one count, a court may return a verdict of guilty on all counts. The primary issue for the Chamber in such a situation is to determine how the matter is to be resolved on sentence. Counts 1, 2 and 3 of the indictment relate to a variety of offences, namely, wilfully causing great suffering, cruel treatment, and inhumane acts. These offences are not strictly cumulative because the continuing course of conduct from the moment the victims are removed from their hospital beds, to when they are beaten at Ovcara farm and while they are transported and waiting to be murdered, may at different moments of time constitute different offences. In other words, the removal of sick people from their hospital beds is an inhumane act, but may not constitute wilfully causing great suffering. On the other hand, to beat someone to the point where they are almost dead, would certainly amount to great suffering. The psychological trauma of being stood up with fellow victims at the edge of a mass grave site waiting to be shot would amount to cruel treatment. The wilful killing and murders in counts 4, 5 and 6 do arise out of the same circumstances, namely where the victims were shot or otherwise killed. The elements of the murders and wilful killings may be similar, but beyond that, there are other required elements which make them very different crimes. One act of murder may violate the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions, the laws and customs of war, and crimes against humanity. The object and purpose of the grave breach provisions is to govern specific aspects of the conduct of armed conflict and to protect certain groups of persons. For example, the main object of the Fourth Geneva Convention is to protect a strictly defined category of civilians from arbitrary action on the part of the enemy. The fundamental principles of the law and customs of war enumerated in the language of common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and embraced by Article 3 of our Statute, provide the minimum rules of conduct applicable to all armed conflict regardless of classification. These minimum rules cover a wider class of actor and provide a wider category of persons than the grave breach provisions. They are essential rules of humanity recognised by all civilised nations, and their purpose is to ensure the humane and non-discriminatory treatment of all non-combatants or persons not involved in the armed conflict. The principal purpose of crimes against humanity has no relation in its core to the conduct of armed conflicts. Rather, it is to ensure the right of diverse parts of civilian populations to exist. An essential element of the crime against humanity is the protection of the members of a civilian population from a widespread and systematic attack. Because each of these articles has a distinct purpose and object and as a consequence, contain different elements. It is permissible that they be charged together in an instance where a particular act is violative of each, and if the accused is guilty, he or she should be subject to a conviction for each. It may well be that for the purposes of sentencing, the various offences are merged for a unified sentence. The essential point inherent in allowing for multiple convictions is that each crime exists to protect certain society norms and each must be valued and preserved. Each of the items charged in the indictment represent these most serious offences. There is a significant interest for the community of nations to ensure that the purpose and prohibitions of each article is respected and prosecuted in the instance where the evidence so warrants. There should be no instance where an accused should be free from responsibility for violating one of these offences simply because his or her conduct is also violative of the other articles as well. There should be no issue of expediency or economy where one of these offences is concerned. If there is a consolidation for sentencing purposes, then there is no significant prejudice to the accused, yet the interests of the community of nations in preserving the purposes of these articles is respected. When this matter was considered in the Tadic case, the Trial Chamber decided that the issue of cumulative charges was only relevant to penalty should the accused be convicted. This reasoning was subsequently applied in rejecting motions on the form of the indictment in the Celebici case. It is also significant to note the value of cumulative charging in circumstances where lesser included offences are not part of the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, as was held to be so by the Trial Chamber in the Tadic case. In conclusion, it is the submission of the Prosecution that the evidence you are about to hear will prove to you beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused is guilty of the offences charged, both as a principal in the case of counts 1, 2 and 3, and as an accomplice to the killings in counts 4, 5 and 6. The accused knew what the purpose of the entire scheme was and by his actions and presence expressed his willingness to be associated with and to contribute to this overall aim. With respect to this crime, of which there is absolutely no doubt, this monstrous atrocity which invokes memories of the worst outrages of World War II borders on the inexplicable. Nothing will ever justify this contemptible abomination. The Harrowing detail of this hideous massacre brought to life through the evidence of the survivors will long echo in the halls and corridors of this institution, but by this course will never be hidden from view. If the accused be found guilty for his part in this crime, then it should only be after he has been afford all of the rights and protections of a fair trial which rights and protections the Prosecution unequivocally supports and upholds, because it is only through justice that a lasting peace in this troubled part of the world can be assured. If your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We still have five minutes so if you do not mind I would like to ask you very quickly two questions but I will not ask you to answer these questions, not today, in any case, not even tomorrow. I wonder whether you could be so kind as to file maybe in two weeks' time, a specific legal brief, as you suggested, actually two specific legal briefs on the -- addressing those points as you suggested in your pre-trial brief. Now, my two points are as follows, and I will try to speak as fast as possible; one point relates to what you just said a few minutes ago about the accumulation of criminal charges. There, again, I am puzzled. I wonder whether, in international criminal law this accumulation of criminal charges is permissible. In other words, can one be charged and convicted for the same action characterised as both, say grave breach and a war crime, or both as a war crime and crime against humanity, or both as a crime against humanity and genocide, for instance? In particular, I would like to know whether this is not contrary -- whether or not it is contrary to the substantive principle, in idem. I wonder whether the Prosecutor could be so kind as to file a brief on this point with the relevant case law, national or international and possibly references to authorities, to legal authorities, in particular in the legal literature. My second question relates to another tricky legal issue, namely internal versus international armed conflict; civil war, international armed conflict. Now, it is alleged that in 1991 there was in Eastern Slavonia an armed conflict which might be regarded as having a mixed nature. A local rebellion against the central authorities, and the armed invasion of JNA. In this second respect, of course, this would be an international armed conflict. Now, the accused is alleged to have been part of a group of local rebels as a civilian authority. Now, my question is as follows; on what legal grounds could be accused of committing criminal offences in the context of an international armed conflict? Let me be more specific. I will ask you the following questions: is the fact of being integrated into the military structure of the occupying army the decisive legal factor in this respect? Or, can one be responsible for grave breaches if he acts as an agent of a foreign army or, one could say, as a defacto organ of a foreign army, so either agent or organ. Or must one be under the control, defacto control of the following army or part and parcel of the chain of command? I wonder whether you could be so kind as to address this specific legal issues. Thank you. Now, we must adjourn now. Tomorrow we will sit at 8.30 sharp. I will make sure that tomorrow the Dutch police will not make the mistakes they made today, so we will start at 8.30, but with a hearing in closed session. I suggest that tomorrow in this hearing, closed session, we should go through the various motions, preliminary motions which have been filed, and some of them are confidential so therefore we must have a private -- a closed session. Our guess is that we need two hours, then there will be probably a coffee break if possible we will make a ruling from the bench, and then we will start at 11 o'clock in open session with the first witnesses called by the Prosecutor. The hearing is adjourned.
